analysis:
Production change is limited to ProviderLoop+Lifecycle.swift (head lines 103-110 and 119). The graceful drain previously required a coordinator acknowledgement, or a nil coordinatorClient, before reporting .drained. It now also accepts the drain when the client exists but hasRegisteredConnection() is false, via the new coordinatorSettled flag. I found no security regression.

The other drain gates are unchanged:
- nativeOwnersDrained and lifecycleRemaining == 0 are still required, so accepted requests are never truncated; only the coordinator ACK is waived.
- The App Attest worker retirement check (workerRetired, line 113) still precedes the outcome decision.
- Admission stays refused (servingDrain.begin, state.refusingNewWork).
- Force semantics are untouched.

The waiver applies only when there is no registered session. In that state a disconnect has already cancelled accepted work and outbound messages are not carried to a later connection (per the code comment, which I did not verify in CoordinatorClient). The ACK therefore has nothing left to confirm. A coordinator cannot exploit this, because it is trusted and no provider or consumer input influences the check. A malicious provider operator gains nothing, since drain only makes the provider stop serving. Remote credential revocation semantics (A-008) are separate from drain.

Open integration questions (out of the supplied evidence): the implementation of CoordinatorClient.hasRegisteredConnection() and CoordinatorConnectionHandshake.start, and the handshakeTimeout config. The handshake-deadline production source is not in this batch, so only its tests were seen. These tests use a loopback silent peer and add no attack surface. Regarding T-010, a race remains possible where a session is registered between the ACK wait and the check, but that case yields true from hasRegisteredConnection() and so keeps the drain at .timedOut, which fails safe. The test changes are test-only. The mailbox and ProcessIdentity validation is unchanged.
